White tern (Gygis alba) chicks emerge from eggs incubated under conditions that closely mimic the natural thermal regime of tropical seabird colonies. When eggs are artificially incubated at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], hatching occurs after approximately 36 days [ab = approximately 36 days], a duration that aligns well with field observations of parental incubation shifts in the species. The newly hatched nestling is surprisingly light, weighing just 16 grams [Wwb = 16 grams] at the moment of emergence, a value that reflects the relatively small egg size characteristic of this species compared to other terns of similar adult dimensions. This low birth mass imposes a steep energetic challenge on the provisioning adults, who must deliver frequent meals of small fish and squid to meet the rapid growth demands of the altricial chick during the first weeks of life. The initial fragility of the neonate is offset by intense biparental care, which buffers the vulnerable young against thermal stress and predation during the critical early developmental window.

By the time the developing chick reaches the point of fledging, it has undergone a dramatic transformation in body composition and size. Under the thermal conditions typical of active metabolic periods for this species, estimated at 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C], young birds achieve their first sustained flight at 80 days after hatching [tx = 80 days after hatching]. This relatively prolonged fledging period, compared to many other terns, may be linked to the species' unique tree-nesting strategy, which requires a higher degree of neuromuscular coordination for safe departure from an arboreal perch. During the intervening weeks, the chick's body mass increases from its natal value of 16 grams to an ultimate adult wet weight of 125 grams [Wwi = 125 grams], representing an approximately eight-fold increase. This asymptotic mass is attained through a combination of rapid skeletal growth and the accumulation of flight muscle and fat reserves essential for the energetically demanding post-fledging period of aerial foraging and dispersal.

The attainment of sexual maturity in the White tern is not simultaneous with the achievement of adult body size, instead occurring after a protracted period of somatic development and social learning. Records indicate that puberty, defined here as the onset of gonadal activity, is reached at 240 days after hatching [tp = 240 days after hatching] under the species' characteristic thermoregulatory conditions of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]. This timing implies that young birds undergo several months of post-fledging maturation before their reproductive systems become fully functional. The delayed onset of puberty relative to fledging likely reflects the need for juveniles to master complex aerial hunting techniques and establish foraging territories adequate to support the energetic demands of egg production and chick provisioning. Such a life-history schedule is consistent with the pattern observed in other long-lived seabirds, where early investment in somatic growth and skill acquisition precedes reproductive effort.

First reproduction in the White tern is further deferred well past the point of initial gonadal maturation, a pattern that underscores the species' slow, K-selected life-history strategy. Age at first breeding, measured as the time since birth at first brood, has been documented at 1764 days [tR = 1764 days] in populations maintained under field conditions, with an associated ambient temperature of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]. This nearly five-year delay before laying the first egg is exceptionally long for a tern, although it finds parallels in the life histories of noddies (Anous spp.) and other tropical seabirds that inhabit resource-poor oceanic environments. The extended pre-breeding period likely reflects the need for individuals to acquire substantial body condition and to secure stable nesting territories in crowded colony settings, where competition for suitable forked branches or man-made structures is intense. Once breeding commences, the reproductive output remains modest, with females producing a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch] and typically raising just one brood annually [F_R_i = one brood annually], resulting in a maximum daily reproductive rate of approximately one offspring every 365 days when considered across the entire breeding season.

Longevity records for the White tern indicate that this species is capable of remarkable survival over decadal timescales, a trait that is typical of tropical seabirds facing low extrinsic mortality. The maximum recorded lifespan is approximately 13,104 days [am = approximately 13,104 days] when measured under the thermal conditions of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C] that characterize its active metabolic state, which translates to roughly 35.9 years [am = roughly 35.9 years]. This exceptional longevity is consistent with the species' slow life-history pace: late age at first reproduction, a single-egg clutch, and a low annual reproductive rate are all hallmarks of a strategy that prioritizes adult survival over high fecundity. The cumulative lifetime reproductive output, though modest on an annual basis, can therefore be substantial when summed over a multi-decade lifespan. Such a life-history syndrome is advantageous in the stable, low-predation environments of remote oceanic islands where the White tern breeds, but it renders the species particularly vulnerable to novel anthropogenic threats such as introduced predators and habitat degradation that increase adult mortality rates.
